name: MEDALLION FINANCIAL CORP

devils_advocate.strongest_counter: The bull case is the CECL argument above and it is genuinely strong, because it is the standard mechanical consequence of record origination growth: under CECL a lender books the lifetime expected loss on a new loan in the quarter it originates it, while the interest arrives over years. Medallion grew loans 7% sequentially to record levels; the provision that growth forces is not evidence of credit deterioration, it is evidence of growth. On that reading H1 2026 earnings are artificially depressed by the very thing that makes the franchise more valuable, and the 10.3% I am calling sustainable is a trough. This also happens to be the counter that the 2026-09-02 pass on this name explicitly could not resolve, and it deserves to be taken seriously rather than waved at.
devils_advocate.what_would_prove_it: Separating the provision into the CECL build on new originations from the charge-offs on the existing book: if net charge-offs are flat and the provision is all growth-driven, the counter wins; if charge-offs are rising, it does not.
devils_advocate.already_visible: Yes, and it does not win. Net charge-offs in recreation lending are disclosed at 3.25% and 3.94% of average gross loans — mid-to-high 3% is realised loss, not a forward reserve, and it is the single largest consumer book. Cumulative taxi-medallion charge-offs also rose $6.6 million year over year, in a portfolio that is supposed to be finished. And the decline is not one quarter of CECL noise: it runs from H2 2025 (roughly $19.9 million implied) through Q1 and Q2 2026, four consecutive periods. The 2026-09-02 pass wrote that its dismissal would fail 'if the ROTCE is real at even 18% — the LOW end of the observed range'. The actual print is 10.3%, which is BELOW the low end of the range, not at it. The test that pass nominated has now been run and it goes the other way.
devils_advocate.unresolved: The cost of equity, which the schema cannot override and which decides the sign. The 8.4% comes from a beta of 0.617 measured at R-squared 0.187 on a stock that trades $701 thousand a day; on that tape it is not a measurement. At 8.4% the corrected gap is +13%; at a beta of 1.0 it is -15%. I also could not size the Series G reopening, so I cannot quantify how much further the NCI dividend load rises.

what_changed: Two things, and the first settles a question two previous passes on this name left open. (1) EARNINGS HAVE COLLAPSED. Q2 2026 net income attributable to Medallion Financial Corp. was $7,445 thousand against $11,069 thousand a year earlier (-33%), and H1 2026 was $12,398 thousand against $23,083 thousand (-46%) — this against RECORD originations, 7% sequential loan growth, total assets through $3.2 billion and net interest income of $57.2 million. The company's own framing is that net income dipped on 'higher provisions and operating expenses'. Recreation-lending net charge-offs are disclosed at 3.25% and 3.94% of average gross loans excluding loans held for sale. Cumulative taxi-medallion net charge-offs rose to $168.1 million from $161.5 million. (2) On 2026-09-22 — the day before this screen — Medallion Bank launched a REOPENING of its Series G non-cumulative perpetual preferred (Nasdaq: MBNKO), proceeds possibly to redeem the Series E. That is more non-controlling-interest capital ahead of the common, and it is what earned this name its opportunistic slot.
consensus_case: At $11.95 Medallion Financial trades at about 1.15x a tangible book of $10.38 a share, which is roughly what a subprime-adjacent consumer lender earning 10% on tangible common equity is worth against an equity cost anywhere north of 8%. The market is not refusing to pay for a 22.6% return — it is correctly pricing the return the company is actually producing NOW. Net income attributable to Medallion Financial fell 46% in the first half of 2026, to $12.4 million from $23.1 million, while originations hit records: the balance sheet is growing and the earnings on it are not, because provisions and operating expense are absorbing the spread. Recreation-lending net charge-offs are running in the 3.25%-3.94% range. A buyer at 1.15x tangible book is paying an ordinary multiple for an ordinary return in a deteriorating credit environment, and there is no free lunch in it.
base_case_rationale: A book-method name, so the input is a sustainable return on tangible common equity, and I set it at 10.5%. H1 2026 net income attributable to the parent of $12.4 million annualises to $24.8 million; tangible common equity is $408.6 million of parent-only stockholders' equity less $150.8 million of goodwill and $17.0 million of intangibles, or $240.8 million. That is a 10.3% return, and I round to 10.5% to avoid pretending to precision on a half-year. The engine's 22.6% is the mean of three GAAP years ending 2025-12-31 — a window that closed before the deterioration began, since FY2025's own second half was already running at roughly $19.9 million against the $23.1 million of H1 2025. This is the CBT/CASH failure on a book-method name: the fiscal window is recent enough that no staleness flag fires, and the business inside it has changed. Note the direction of travel is still downward, so 10.5% is a current reading and not obviously a floor.
key_risks: Net income attributable to the parent fell 46% year over year in H1 2026 and the trend is not yet arrested
Recreation-lending net charge-offs at 3.25%-3.94% into a softening consumer, on 2024-25 vintages that are only part-seasoned
Goodwill and intangibles are 41% of reported book; strip them and the equity cushion is $240.8M against $3.2B of assets
The Series G preferred reopening adds non-controlling-interest dividends ahead of the common, and the NCI already took $4.7M of H1 earnings
$701K average daily dollar volume — a position could not be exited quickly, and the 0.62 beta setting the 8.4% cost of equity is measured on that tape
watch_for: Q3 2026 net income attributable to Medallion Financial Corp.: a print below ~$7M confirms the trend rather than a CECL artifact
Recreation-lending net charge-off ratio: whether it holds below 4% or breaks above it
Size and pricing of the Series G reopening, and whether the Series E is actually redeemed
Any decomposition of provision expense into growth-driven CECL build versus realised loss
